label: copy-phase input j (fed-back j at original position >= 1)
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase, when the fed-back input token is j, i.e. j is being re-read as original token recall_idx-1 with recall_idx >= 2. It never fires on j during the original phase, at the delimiter, on the first two copy steps, or on any other input token. Every activation falls inside the predicate (recall 1.0). Magnitude is largest when the j sits at original position 2-3 (recall_idx 3-4) early in the copy; it is weaker at later positions and on the second j of a jj run (often zero there). Most false positives are repeated j, j at recall_idx 2, or j at the final step.

issues: Reproduced the test scores: precision 0.829, recall 1.0, F1 0.907, mass recall 1.0. Dev and test misses both show 0 missed activations. Activation is zero in the original and delimiter phases and on every token other than j.

Precision of j in the copy phase by recall_idx: r=1 0.0, r=2 0.565, r=3 0.981, r=4 0.977, r=5 0.886, r=6 0.777, r=7 0.793, r=8 0.795. This supports 'strongest at original positions 2-3, weaker later'. r=2 (j at original position 1) is the weakest included case.
Repeated j is weaker, as claimed: precision is 0.63 when prev_tok==j and 0.77 when in_count>1.

One minor inaccuracy: the explanation says false positives cluster at the final step, but to_go==0 has precision 0.818, about the same as the overall 0.829. The final step is not a distinct false-positive class.

I found no systematic false-positive class. Splits by n_digits, first_tok (letter vs digit), L at r=2, and previous token being a vowel or digit all change precision by only a few points. The remaining false positives look like a diffuse threshold effect, concentrated at r=2 and r>=5.
